12.0.0.en: 1- "Help, Lord; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men."

12.0.1.en: 1- David remembers the injustices of Saul against him, and of the Philistines too, and every wrong that falls upon the children of God, so he cries out to the Lord saying "Help, Lord"; because there is no hope for the poor in affliction except God.

12.0.2.en: 2- "The godly man ceaseth", that is, the number of those who fear God, who walk in righteousness, has become very small as a result of the wrong done to them by the wicked: some died and others feared people, so they abandoned righteousness. And the wicked try to wipe out the righteous so that they will not condemn them by their goodness, and so the wicked rid themselves of the pricking of conscience, since Satan makes them feel that the evil they do is the natural behavior of people.

12.0.3.en: 3- "The faithful fail from among the children of men", that is, the number of the faithful in business dealings has become very small, as well as the faithful in holding fast to the faith and the creed, so that the majority has become tainted with strange ideas and doubts.

12.0.4.en: 4- David asks for salvation because of the spread of evil in the world, and this salvation was accomplished in the fullness of time by the Incarnation of Christ the Savior. Elijah felt the same feelings as David, when he said that all had gone astray and he alone was left, and God reassured him that there were seven thousand knees that had not bowed to Baal (1 Kgs 19:18).

12.1.0.en: 2- "They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak." Flattering: from flattery, which is showing something other than what a person holds within, in order to deceive the listener with false praise. A double heart: the wicked man has two hearts, meaning two faces, so he speaks deceitfully to the listener although inside him are opposite feelings.

12.1.1.en: 1- The wicked are liars because they show other than what they hold within; they speak words of praise to others although they hate them in their hearts, or they reassure them when the matter calls for caution; this is so as to make them fall into the trap, for the purpose of the words of the wicked is to deceive the righteous and make them fall by malicious plots into many problems in order to be rid of them, and this is a continuation of what the first verse mentioned.

12.1.2.en: 2- Jeremiah set forth the same meaning about the wicked in (Jer 9:4, 5), and Christ Himself rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy (Mt 23), and James the Apostle tells us of the danger of the tongue of the wicked (Jas 3:1-12).

12.2.0.en: 3- "The Lord shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things."

12.2.2.en: 1- The evil of the wicked reached not only to deceit, but to speaking shamelessly of great, shocking sins as though they were an ordinary matter.

12.2.3.en: 2- David the prophet declares that there is a divine threat to the wicked, that God will uproot the deceitful lips and the evil tongue, that is, He will uproot the wicked if they do not repent; so it is a call to repentance, but a firm one, perhaps the wicked will take heed.

12.3.0.en: 4- "Who have said, With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?"

12.3.1.en: 1- He describes these wicked people as proud, whose might and power are in their tongue, although in truth they are deceivers of no worth before the power of God. And they declared that they are free and say what they want.

12.3.2.en: 2- Throughout history wicked people have appeared who neglected the existence of God and were proud, such as Pharaoh (Ex 15:4), whose end was drowning with his army in the Red Sea, and Herod, who accepted praise as a god, so God struck him with worms and he died (Acts 12:23).

12.3.3.en: Do not be troubled by the plots of the wicked and their injustice, for it is temporary and will come to an end. Hold fast to your prayer, for God hears you and is near you, and the troubles He allows for you are for your good, so that you may be purified from your sins, but He keeps you and has prepared for you a great place in the Kingdom.

12.4.0.en: 5- "For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the Lord; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him." (literally: I will set him in a wide place, him who is puffed at)

12.4.1.en: In a wide place: that is, in spaciousness and ease.

12.4.2.en: Him who is puffed at: him upon whom the wicked blow and pour out their wrath and harm him.

12.4.3.en: 1- God is longsuffering toward the wicked, that they may repent, but their persistence in evil makes them use up their opportunity, especially when the poor cry out to God as a result of the injustice of the wicked, and God intervenes swiftly, for He says, "Now will I arise."

12.4.4.en: 2- God does not merely stop the wicked, but also glorifies His righteous poor children and puts them in ease and a spacious, safe life. And this will be declared plainly before all, to strengthen those who fear God and to alert the wicked to repent. And in the Septuagint translation, that is, the Agpeya, it says "I will deal openly in salvation" instead of "I will set him in a wide place, him who is puffed at", that is, the salvation of the wronged poor will be plain before all.

12.4.5.en: 3- This divine threat that God will arise to save the righteous from the hands of the wicked, God carried out many times, such as bringing His people out of the land of Egypt, and drowning Pharaoh and his army in the sea, and also delivering His people from Amalek in their war in the wilderness of Sinai. And delivering His people from the surrounding pagan nations many times, in the days of Joshua, the judges, Saul, David and Solomon.

12.4.6.en: 4- This open divine salvation Christ accomplished in the fullness of time on the Cross, and He will also declare it with power on the Day of Judgment before all mankind, from Adam to the end of the ages.

12.5.0.en: 6- "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times."

12.5.1.en: 1- If the words of the wicked are deceit, flattery and hypocrisy, the words of God are pure, and they purify those who hear them, as Christ Himself said, "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you" (Jn 15:3).

12.5.2.en: 2- The words of God are pure like silver that is refined in the furnace seven times, that is, a complete refining. This shows how pure the words of God are, since they have no impurities. And Christ in His Sermon on the Mount spoke the first seven Beatitudes, which are found in the one who receives the eighth Beatitude, which is persecution; that is, one cannot reach the eighth Beatitude unless a person is purified by the first seven Beatitudes.

12.6.0.en: 7- "Thou shalt keep them, O Lord, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever."

12.6.1.en: 1- David the prophet declares that God keeps and guards His righteous children from the hands of the wicked, so no affliction befalls them except what God allows for their benefit; they are under God's protection throughout their life in this age, and this gives them reassurance, so they move freely in their relationship with God and their service to Him.

12.6.2.en: 2- The prophet promises the humble righteous, that is, the poor, that God will keep them with Him for ever, and even give them the enjoyment of fellowship with Him in the Kingdom of Heaven, so they enjoy God throughout their life, and then in heaven. This is contrary to the wicked, who live in turmoil and when they die go to eternal torment. Therefore the title of this psalm says "to the end, for the eighth", that is, God keeps the life of the righteous on earth and gives them the enjoyment of the glories of the Kingdom, which the eighth day symbolizes.

12.7.0.en: 8- "The wicked walk on every side, when the vilest men are exalted."

12.7.1.en: Walk on every side: they spread throughout the whole world.

12.7.2.en: 1- After David concluded the psalm in the seventh verse with God's care for His children, he returns in the last verse, the eighth, here, and declares that the wicked will remain spread in every place in the world, and most of them will not repent, so that the righteous may not be shaken by the spread of evil, but stand firm and lean on God, who protects them.

12.7.3.en: 2- The wicked will support one another when some of them take great authority in the world, so they encourage evil, and sins spread, and even become the law of the world, but all this does not make the children of God troubled; because Christ said, "The whole world lieth in wickedness" (1 Jn 5:19).

12.7.4.en: God hears your petition, especially when you are in severe affliction, and hastens to you, so do not despair, but seek Him with faith and persistence, for He is able to rescue you from every evil, however it surrounds you.

12.7.5.en: Taking refuge in God. For the choir director. A psalm of David. "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord?"... (v. 1). Introduction:

12.7.6.en: 1- The writer of this psalm is David the prophet.

12.7.9.en: a - When David was fleeing from the face of Saul, and Saul was placing watchers on him everywhere, and pursuing him with great armies to seize him, and at some times he almost seized him, but at the last moment God delivered him.

12.7.10.en: b - When David fell into his great sins such as adultery and murder, and felt severe distress, as though God had left him, and he cried out to Him.

12.7.11.en: c - When his son Absalom rose against him and drove him from the kingdom, and went out to fight him, trying to kill him.

12.7.12.en: 3- This psalm is repeated collectively because it is titled "for the choir director", that is, a group of singers who have a leader.

12.7.13.en: 4- It is a short prayer that the man of God cries out in severe affliction, and it includes the basic aspects of prayer, which are complaint, supplication and praise.

12.7.14.en: 5- It speaks in the spirit of prophecy about the affliction that meets the people of God, which is the captivity and humiliation four times at the hands of the kingdoms: Assyria and Babylon, then Media and Persia, and after them Greece; therefore David repeats an important question to God, which is "How long", four times.

12.7.15.en: 6- This psalm is a symbol of the afflictions that come upon a person from every side in his life, that is, from the four directions of the world, so we find that it repeated "How long" four times.

12.7.16.en: 7- This psalm is said in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime.

13.0.0.en: 1- "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?"

13.0.1.en: 1- David does not ask an interrogative question when he says "How long?", but implores God with all his heart and reproaches Him, since he feels that He has neglected him and left him, and even feels that He has hidden His face from him; because of his sin and weakness, or because problems and afflictions surround him.

13.0.2.en: 2- David, despite his feeling that God is not with him because of the pressure of the affliction upon him, has hope in Him that He will save him; therefore he cried out to Him, "How long wilt thou forget me?"

13.0.3.en: 3- A person in his spiritual lukewarmness feels that God has neglected him, although God withdraws a little so that the person may strive and seek after God, and so experience new depths of His love.

13.0.4.en: 4- Satan fights a person in affliction, making him imagine that God may forget him utterly, or "to the end" according to the Septuagint translation, so that he falls into despair; but the beautiful thing about David is that he did not give in, but rose to pray in reproaching God, that He may rescue him from the affliction.

13.0.5.en: 5- David had become accustomed to fellowship with God; therefore he felt that God had hidden His face from him, so he was greatly distressed and offered repentance and prayer to regain his sense of God, who is his life. But the person who is far from God does not feel these feelings and does not seek God with this persistence.

13.0.6.en: 6- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who said on the Cross, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Mt 27:46), so from this aspect it is considered among the Messianic psalms.

13.0.7.en: 7- We notice that David did not complain about Saul, or Absalom, or any difficult circumstances surrounding him, but directed his complaint to God, saying "How long wilt thou forget me?", since he feels that God's presence with him is enough for him and protects him and rescues him from any affliction; he is not distressed by people, but he needs God.

13.1.0.en: 2- "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?"

13.1.1.en: 1- After David reproached God in the first verse with the first reproach, which is neglect and forgetfulness, and reproached Him with the second reproach, which is hiding His face from him, here he reproaches Him with the third reproach, which is that his heart has been filled with cares and sorrow, as a result of his sin and the severity of the affliction upon him; David's thoughts, which Satan stirs up, press upon him, so that he is depressed under the weight of thoughts of care and fear.

13.1.2.en: 2- David reproaches God with the fourth reproach, saying: why have You allowed my enemy, who is Satan, to prevail over me and humble me? This is a confession of his weakness and faith in the power of God, who is able to drive his enemy away from him.

13.1.3.en: 3- David advances in his cry to God in four stages:

13.1.4.en: a - His feeling of God's neglect of him.

13.1.5.en: b - His sense of losing the sight of God and fellowship with Him; because He has hidden His face from him.

13.1.6.en: c - The filling of his heart with evil thoughts of cares and sorrow.

13.1.7.en: d - His distress at the enemy's triumph over him.

13.1.8.en: But despite all this he has hope in God, and cries out to Him to rescue him from all these troubles, which advanced gradually, as we mentioned; for a sin that advances gradually, God is able to remove it and all its results.

13.1.9.en: 4- David represents the spiritual man, who finds rest only in the arms of God; whatever David's resources and strength, he seeks the face of God, who satisfies him and delivers him from all troubles, since fellowship with God is his life and there is no substitute for it in the wealth of the world or its power; for if he has all the resources and does not have God with him, he is in great affliction.

13.1.10.en: 5- God does not forget man, but man in his sin feels that God has forgotten him, but through prayer he regains his sense of God.

13.1.11.en: 6- Anxiety, care and the feeling of losing God is a natural result of sin, and this is considered a divine grace, since it drives the spiritual person to prayer, so that he regains his life with God.

13.1.12.en: When affliction comes upon you, seek God and press Him, until He intervenes and restores your peace and makes you feel His presence, whether by removing the affliction at once, or leaving it for a time, but you will rejoice in your sense that God is with you.

13.1.13.en: (2) Asking for the help of A (vv. 3, 4:)

13.2.0.en: 3- "Consider and hear me, O Lord my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death."

13.2.1.en: 1- David addresses God, "Consider", meaning that He should look upon his lowliness and need, the enemy's insolence against him, and his repentance, so that He may rescue him because he is His son, and he has no hope except in Him.

13.2.2.en: 2- David believes that God is his heavenly Father, who will feel for him and answer his prayer; therefore he demands of Him, "Hear me", and says to Him "my God": You are the Lord, the master of all kingdoms, but You are also my God who loves me, and cannot bear to see me in this weakness and lowliness. You are able, O God, to do all things, and at the same time You love me with perfect love, and give me special care because I am Your son.

13.2.3.en: 3- David also asks God to lighten his eyes, that is, to give him spiritual enlightenment, which is the knowledge of God, so that he may come out of his spiritual lukewarmness and be rid of his sin, which separates him from God.

13.2.4.en: 4- This enlightenment is life for David and without it he dies, for there is no life without the knowledge of God. On the other hand he asks God to hasten to lighten his eyes, before he is swallowed up by sorrow and grows weak before his enemy and he destroys him, that is, he asks for the power of God and His light to protect him from the demons.

13.2.5.en: 5- Spiritual enlightenment is able to restore confidence to David's soul, and spiritual zeal, and remove sorrows, and cast the enemy down under his feet, that is, it answers all four degrees of sin mentioned before in (vv. 1, 2).

13.3.0.en: 4- "Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; and those that trouble me rejoice when I am moved."

13.3.1.en: 1- David demands that God intervene, lest the principles be overturned by the triumph of Satan, so that he thinks he is stronger than the children of God and that he has been able to shake them and drive them away from God. So he asks God to intervene for the following:

13.3.2.en: a - For the glory of God's name.

13.3.3.en: b - To rescue him from destruction.

13.3.4.en: c - So that the righteous may stand firm in righteousness and not doubt.

13.3.5.en: d - To put the wicked to shame so that they repent.

13.3.6.en: 2- As heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents, the demons on the other hand rejoice at the destruction of one righteous man and shout for joy; therefore David demands that God intervene swiftly, to stop the joy of the wicked at the destruction of the righteous.

13.3.7.en: The devil has no authority over you, so if you fall, rise and ask God to drive him away from you and rescue you, and even raise you up, so that you experience fellowship with Him, and He lightens your eyes, and you make up for all that you have missed.

13.4.0.en: 5- "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation."

13.4.1.en: 1- Since David pleaded with God in (vv. 3, 4) and asked for spiritual enlightenment, he placed all his trust in the mercy of God, so he became settled psychologically and spiritually and felt reassurance, and his heart found rest; because he did not trust in any human power, but in God, who is able to do all things and abundant in mercies, who forgives every sin.

13.4.2.en: 2- After the reassurance, David felt joy at his sense of God's work with him, who rescued him from his enemy and from all his evil thoughts, and forgave his sins.

13.4.3.en: 3- In the spirit of prophecy David saw Christ the Savior, and his heart rejoiced in the complete salvation on the Cross.

13.4.4.en: 4- Here we see the power of prayer, which transforms a person from severe sorrow and complaint to God into supplication with confidence and asking for enlightenment, then trust, and finally joy.

13.5.0.en: 6- "I will sing unto the Lord, because he hath dealt bountifully with me."

13.5.1.en: 1- David felt the grace of God, His forgiveness, His support and His great kindness to him; therefore he lifted up his heart with thanksgiving, praise and song.

13.5.2.en: 2- The faith of David appears, for although the affliction was not outwardly removed, he received peace of heart through his faith, so he thanked God and praised Him, and after this God's work in him was completed and He lifted him up and glorified him.

13.5.3.en: 3- Although the psalm is brief and small, it includes all the feelings of a person in affliction, and the work of God in the heart, until He gladdens him in the end; so it is suitable for prayer in all afflictions.

13.5.4.en: How beautiful is the thanksgiving and praise that you offer to God when He works in your life, for it establishes your faith, and gladdens your heart, and gladdens the heart of God.

13.5.5.en: The danger of denying God. For the choir director. Of David. "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God"... (v. 1). Introduction:

13.5.6.en: 1- Its writer: David, and he used to sing the psalm with a group of singers who have a director, that is, a leader.

13.5.7.en: 2- The occasion of the writing of the psalm

13.5.8.en: a - A prophecy about Sennacherib, who reproached God and His people in the days of the reign of King Hezekiah.

13.5.9.en: b - A prophecy about Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who took the kingdom of Judah captive and reproached God and His people.

13.5.10.en: c - The rejection of the corruption of those who deny God in every generation.

13.5.11.en: 3- The psalm shows the causes of the corruption of the atheists, and examines their psychology and their evils, and the saving power of God for His people from their hand.

13.5.12.en: 4- This psalm resembles Psalm 53 and does not differ from it except in a few words, and perhaps the reason is the repetition of the idea in David's mind and his distress at the evils of the atheists.

13.5.13.en: 5- Paul the Apostle quoted from this psalm (Rom 3:10-13), to show that the Jews and the Gentiles had both gone away from the knowledge of God and were immersed in evil.

13.5.14.en: 6- This psalm bears a prophecy about Christ the Savior (v. 7), so it can be considered among the Messianic psalms.

13.5.15.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
